communityImage.caption: Bosnians in the Rochester area gather to mark the 30th anniversary of the Srebrenica genocide, July 2025.

people.name: Elvis Budimlic
body: In February 1993, in an office in Zagreb, Croatia, 20-year-old Elvis Budimlic sat across from a United Nations refugee official who asked where in the world he wanted to go. He noticed a copy of Money magazine lying nearby. The magazine regularly named Rochester, Minnesota, among its Best Places to Live. That settled it.

To understand why he was in that office, it helps to know what happened in northwest Bosnia in 1992. Serb forces took control of the Prijedor region and held non-Serb civilians in camps. His brother Armin told the Post Bulletin in 2023 that close to 4,000 people were killed in Prijedor and the neighboring county. Elvis, still a teenager, was taken from his home by soldiers and spent about 200 days in concentration camps, including Omarska.

In June 1993 Elvis and his wife, Sebiha, arrived in Rochester with sponsorship from Catholic Charities. By his brother Armin's account, Elvis was the first Bosnian refugee in Rochester. His sister and her family followed six months later, then his brother Armin with his wife and children, and later his mother and oldest brother. Friends came, and friends of friends. Catholic Charities counted 67 Bosnian refugees relocated to Rochester from June 1993 through 1996. The Post Bulletin's 2024 estimate is 600 to 1,000 Bosnians living in the city today.
Elvis also helped the people who came after him. Working part time as a case manager for the Intercultural Mutual Assistance Association, he knew all 67 by name.
A chance glance at a magazine became the starting point of one of Minnesota's Bosnian communities, built by survivors who turned a city they had read about into a home.
keyFacts: 1992: Taken from his home by soldiers; about 200 days in camps, including Omarska.
February 1993: Interviewed in Zagreb and chose Rochester after seeing a Money magazine ranking.
June 1993: Arrived in Rochester with his wife, Sebiha, sponsored by Catholic Charities.
June 1993 to 1996: 67 Bosnian refugees relocated to Rochester, by Catholic Charities' count.
Worked part time as a case manager for the Intercultural Mutual Assistance Association.
people.connectToWork: When someone tells you where their relatives live, how could that change who you plan with, and which services and supports you ask them about?

people.name: Armin Budimlic
body: As a teenager in Prijedor, in what was then Yugoslavia, Armin Budimlic learned English from rock music and from American TV shows like Dallas and Dynasty. His father worked at a paper factory and his mother cared for six children. The language he picked up from pop culture later helped him build a life in a Minnesota city.

When war broke out in 1992, Armin was working in neighboring Croatia, and communication was cut. His wife, Samka, and their 3-year-old daughter reached the Croatia–Bosnia border, and he found them and brought them to Croatia, where the family spent time in a refugee camp. His younger brother Elvis was held in camps in Bosnia.
After Elvis was resettled in Rochester in 1993, the family followed in stages. Armin arrived in 1994 with his wife and two children. Today about 30 of his relatives live in the Rochester area.

Armin had studied mechanical engineering in Bosnia. In Rochester he joined the Intercultural Mutual Assistance Association in 1998 to help fellow Bosnians resettle. He became a U.S. citizen in 2000, and earned a business administration degree at Rochester Community and Technical College, a bachelor's degree at Winona State University and, in 2009, an MBA from Saint Mary's University. As of October 2026 he is the association's executive director. It now serves refugees and immigrants from many countries across southeast Minnesota. In 2021 the Minnesota Department of Human Services gave him a Civic Engagement Award among its Outstanding Refugee Awards.
His career runs from being helped to being the helper. An organization that once received Bosnian newcomers is now led by one of them and serves people who arrived long after him.
keyFacts: 1964: Born in Prijedor, Bosnia and Herzegovina (then Yugoslavia).
1992: Working in Croatia when the war began; reunited with his wife and daughter there.
1994: Arrived in the United States as a refugee with his wife and two children.
1998: Joined the Intercultural Mutual Assistance Association; 2000: U.S. citizen; 2009: MBA, Saint Mary's University.
2021: Civic Engagement Award, Minnesota DHS Outstanding Refugee Awards.
As of October 2026: Executive director of the association.
people.connectToWork: Who in your service area once used the system you work in and now helps run it, and what do they know that your procedures do not capture?

people.name: Aleksandar Hemon
body: In early 1992 a young Sarajevo journalist flew to Chicago on what was meant to be a short visit. That spring war broke out in Bosnia and the siege of Sarajevo began. Aleksandar Hemon could not go home, and he became a refugee in a city far from everything he knew.

He soon began writing, and his work in English drew wide notice. His novel-in-stories Nowhere Man and his novel The Lazarus Project, a 2008 National Book Award finalist, look at displacement, memory and what it means to live between two homes. His memoir, The Book of My Lives, runs from a Sarajevo childhood to an adult life in Chicago.

His honors include a 2003 Guggenheim Fellowship and a 2004 MacArthur Fellowship. He became a U.S. citizen in 2000, and the Carnegie Corporation of New York named him one of its Great Immigrants in 2019. He teaches creative writing at Princeton University, according to his Carnegie and Copper Canyon Press biographies. Copper Canyon says he lives in New Jersey.
His writing shows Sarajevo as a city with its own humor, music and intellectual life, and not only as the war footage many Americans remember.
keyFacts: 1964: Born in Sarajevo.
1992: Arrived in Chicago on a short visit; the war prevented his return.
2000: Became a U.S. citizen.
2003: Guggenheim Fellowship; 2004: MacArthur Fellowship.
2008: The Lazarus Project, National Book Award finalist.
2019: Carnegie Corporation Great Immigrants honoree.
people.connectToWork: What do your intake questions and case notes capture about the life a person had before displacement, and how does that change what you offer them?

people.name: Vedad Ibišević
body: In 2000 a 16-year-old who spoke hardly any English enrolled at Roosevelt High School in south St. Louis. His family had left Bosnia by way of Switzerland and lived in an apartment on Gravois Avenue. Within three years Vedad Ibišević was setting scoring records at Saint Louis University.

He played for the Roosevelt Rough Riders and in suburban club soccer, then joined Saint Louis University. In his only season there, 2003, he scored 18 goals, breaking the school's freshman records and leading all NCAA freshmen in scoring.

In 2004 he left to turn professional with Paris Saint-Germain, a decision his coach said was about helping his family. He played in France and then Germany, where he scored for Hoffenheim and Stuttgart in the Bundesliga. He also played for the Bosnia and Herzegovina national team. St. Louis Magazine counted seven goals for him in 2014 World Cup qualifying as of July 2013, second on the team behind Edin Džeko. The team went on to its first World Cup.
A teenager formed in American public-school and college soccer helped carry Bosnia and Herzegovina onto the world stage.
keyFacts: 2000: Arrived in St. Louis at about 16 after the family left Bosnia by way of Switzerland; enrolled at Roosevelt High School.
2003: Scored 18 goals for Saint Louis University, breaking the school's freshman records.
2004: Signed with Paris Saint-Germain.
Played in the German Bundesliga for Hoffenheim and Stuttgart.
Played for Bosnia and Herzegovina in qualifying for the 2014 World Cup.
people.connectToWork: When a young person's choices are shaped by what the family needs, how do your plans and timelines leave room for that without assuming it?

people.name: Anesa Kajtazović
body: In November 2010 a 24-year-old from Waterloo, Iowa, defeated longtime Waterloo mayor John Rooff to win a seat in the Iowa House of Representatives, with 59 percent of the vote. Anesa Kajtazović became the youngest woman ever elected to the Iowa legislature. The Congress of Bosniaks of North America hailed her as the first Bosniak American elected to the Iowa House.

She was born in Bihać, in northwest Bosnia. Her family fled the war and came to Waterloo as refugees in 1997, when she was about 11. She earned bachelor's degrees in business and public administration from the University of Northern Iowa.

She served in the Iowa House from 2011 to 2015, representing the Waterloo area. In August 2013 she announced a campaign for Congress in Iowa's 1st District, in which, Global Voices noted, she could have become the first Bosnian-born member of Congress. She did not win the nomination.
She arrived as a child refugee and was an elected lawmaker before she turned 25.
keyFacts: 1986: Born in Bihać, Bosnia and Herzegovina (then Yugoslavia).
1997: Family came to Waterloo, Iowa, as refugees.
November 2010: Elected to the Iowa House at 24.
2011 to 2015: Served in the Iowa House.
2013: Announced a campaign for Iowa's 1st Congressional District.

people.name: Amer Kobaslija
body: In 1993 a young art student from Banja Luka fled to Germany from the Bosnian War. Amer Kobaslija kept painting and briefly studied at the Academy of Fine Arts in Düsseldorf. In 1997 his family settled in Florida.

He rebuilt his education in a new country, earning a BFA from Ringling College of Art in 2003 and an MFA from Montclair State University in 2005. A Joan Mitchell Foundation grant came in 2005, a Pollock-Krasner Foundation grant in 2006 and, in 2013, a Guggenheim Fellowship for painting.

His paintings focus on places, often seen from high, camera-like angles. He has painted artists' studios and small rooms, the studio of the painter Balthus in Rossinière, Switzerland, and Kesennuma, Japan, after the 2011 tsunami. More recent Florida portraits and landscapes deal with climate change and urban sprawl.

According to his gallery, his work is held by the Hunter Museum of American Art in Chattanooga, the de Saisset Museum in Santa Clara, the Staten Island Museum and the Embassy of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Brussels. New York's George Adams Gallery represents him. As of October 2026 the University of Central Florida lists him as an associate professor of studio art.
keyFacts: 1975: Born in Banja Luka, Bosnia and Herzegovina (then Yugoslavia).
1993: Fled to Germany; briefly studied in Düsseldorf.
1997: Family settled in Florida.
2003: BFA, Ringling College of Art; 2005: MFA, Montclair State University.
2013: Guggenheim Fellowship.
2019: Shortlisted for the Florida Prize for Contemporary Art.

people.name: Kenan Trebinčević
body: In the spring of 1992 Kenan Trebinčević was 11 and living with his family in Brčko, a town in northeastern Bosnia. Then the war came. His memoir describes friends, neighbors and teammates turning against the family because they were Muslim. His father and brother were held in a concentration camp. The family reached the United States in 1993.

Kenan became a U.S. citizen in 2001 and a physical therapist, and he lives in Astoria, Queens. Two decades after leaving, he agreed to his father's wish that they return to Bosnia together, and he went with a list of things he wanted to do there, including seeing the camp.

That journey became The Bosnia List: A Memoir of War, Exile, and Return, written with Susan Shapiro and published in paperback by Penguin in February 2014. His writing has also appeared in the New York Times Magazine, the Wall Street Journal, Salon and The Best American Travel Writing 2012.
His book gives many American readers a close look at the war through a child's eyes, and an honest account of carrying anger and grief as an adult.
keyFacts: 1980: Born in Brčko, Bosnia and Herzegovina (then Yugoslavia).
1992: War reached Brčko; his father and brother were held in a camp.
1993: Arrived in the United States; 2001: Became a U.S. citizen.
February 25, 2014: The Bosnia List published in paperback by Penguin.
Works as a physical therapist in New York.
people.connectToWork: If someone had good reason to distrust people close to them, including neighbors, what in your process would let them choose who is told what?

people.name: Mirsad Hadžikadić
body: In October 2018 a computer science professor from Charlotte, North Carolina, was in Bosnia, days from an election, running for one of the country's three presidency seats. Mirsad Hadžikadić had lived in the United States for more than three decades. He ran as an independent under the slogan "Bosnia First."

He left Yugoslavia for the United States in 1984 for doctoral study, years before the war, and joined the University of North Carolina at Charlotte in 1987. His path differs from the refugee stories on this page: some Bosnians came to the U.S. as students and professionals before the war.

At UNC Charlotte he became the founding dean of the College of Computing and Informatics, directed the Complex Systems Institute and led data science programs. As of October 2026 the college lists him as a professor emeritus.

In the 2018 race he finished fourth of six candidates for the Bosniak seat, with nearly 10 percent of the vote by WFAE's report, and third in Sarajevo by UNC Charlotte's. He stayed on to build a party, Platform for Progress, and said in 2019 that he intended to run again in 2022.
keyFacts: He was 63 in 2018, according to UNC Charlotte.
1984: Moved to the United States for doctoral study.
1987: Joined UNC Charlotte.

people.name: Flory Jagoda
body: As a teenager in occupied Yugoslavia, the future Flory Jagoda boarded a train out of Sarajevo carrying false papers under a Christian name, and an accordion. Her stepfather told her to play. She played so well that the conductor never asked for her ticket, and she later believed the music saved her life.

She was born in Sarajevo in 1923 into a Sephardic Jewish family whose ancestors had been expelled from Spain in 1492 and settled first in Istanbul. At home they spoke Ladino, or Judeo-Spanish, and she learned songs from her grandmother, her nona. Decades later she learned that most of her family in Bosnia, including her grandmother, had been murdered near Vlasenica.

The European Jewish Congress traces her escape through Split and Korčula and across the Adriatic to Bari, Italy, where she met an American soldier, Harry Jagoda. She moved to the United States in 1946. She went on to perform, teach and compose in Ladino.

Her Hanukkah song "Ocho Kandelikas" has been recorded by artists including Idina Menzel, and her albums include Memories of Sarajevo. In 2002 the National Endowment for the Arts named her a National Heritage Fellow. She died in Alexandria, Virginia, on January 29, 2021, at 97.
She carried a language and a song repertoire across an ocean, after the family who taught them to her had been killed.
keyFacts: 1923: Born in Sarajevo.
World War II: Escaped by train on false papers; most of her family in Bosnia was murdered.
1946: Moved to the United States after marrying Harry Jagoda.
Wrote "Ocho Kandelikas," a widely recorded Hanukkah song.
2002: NEA National Heritage Fellowship.
January 29, 2021: Died in Alexandria, Virginia, at 97.
people.connectToWork: What would you get wrong if you assumed someone's faith, language or history from the country they or their family came from?

people.name: Maja Ruznic
body: At the 2024 Whitney Biennial in New York, one of only a few painters featured was a woman who had spent part of her childhood in refugee camps. Maja Ruznic's large, glowing canvases draw on memories of war, family and migration.

She was born in Bosnia and fled after the war began in 1992. She spent three years in refugee camps before reaching the United States. At nine, in a camp in Austria, she was given a set of watercolors. "I became obsessed with creating worlds," she told Cultured Magazine.

She graduated from the California College of the Arts and now lives in New Mexico. Her work has been shown at the Whitney, the Aspen Art Museum, the Harwood Museum of Art in Taos, SITE Santa Fe and the National Museum in Oslo. Karma gallery represents her and presented her 2024 solo show The World Doesn't End in New York.
A child's years in the camps became a body of work that major museums now show.
keyFacts: 1983: Born in Bosnia and Herzegovina (then Yugoslavia).
From 1992: Three years in refugee camps, including in Austria.
Lives in New Mexico; graduate of the California College of the Arts.
2024: Whitney Biennial; solo show at Karma, New York.
2025: SITE Santa Fe; National Museum, Oslo.

people.name: Luka Garza
body: In February 2021 a center for the University of Iowa passed every Hawkeye before him to become the school's all-time leading scorer. Weeks later Luka Garza was the unanimous national college player of the year. Iowa later retired his No. 55.

Garza was born on December 27, 1998, and grew up in Washington, D.C. His father, Frank, played college basketball at Idaho. His mother, Šejla, comes from Bosnia and Herzegovina and played on a Yugoslavian national team before playing professionally in Europe.
At Iowa from 2017 to 2021 he was a two-time Big Ten Player of the Year and the 2020 winner of the Kareem Abdul-Jabbar Award. He finished with 2,306 points.

The Detroit Pistons drafted him in 2021. In August 2022 he signed with the Minnesota Timberwolves on a two-way contract, which was later converted to a standard NBA contract, and he played in seven games for Minnesota in the 2024 playoffs. As of October 2026 NBA.com lists him with the Boston Celtics.

He also chose to represent his mother's homeland. He joined the Bosnia and Herzegovina national team in 2023 and helped it finish second at an Olympic pre-qualifying tournament, averaging 12.4 points and 7.0 rebounds over five games.
keyFacts: December 27, 1998: Born; grew up in Washington, D.C.
2020–21: Unanimous national college player of the year at Iowa.
February 2021: Became Iowa's all-time leading scorer (2,306 points).
August 2022: Signed with the Minnesota Timberwolves.
2023: First named to the Bosnia and Herzegovina national team.
As of October 2026: On the Boston Celtics roster.
people.connectToWork: How do your forms handle someone whose ties to a community come through a parent rather than a birthplace, and who gets to say they count?

people.name: Adi Granov
body: When director Jon Favreau set out to make the 2008 film Iron Man, he saw the work of a comic book artist and invited him onto the film. That artist was Adi Granov, who had left Sarajevo for America during the Bosnian War.

Granov began his career as a concept artist for Nintendo, working on games such as Bionic Commando and Wave Race: Blue Storm. He began drawing for Marvel in 2003, mainly covers for series such as Iron Man, She-Hulk, Inhumans and Thor. His break came on Iron Man comics, above all the painted Extremis arc written by Warren Ellis.

On the Iron Man films he created concept illustrations, keyframes and designs, working with Marvel Studios and Stan Winston's studio to bring the armor to the screen. He did similar work on The Avengers (2012).

The look of Iron Man that millions of moviegoers know was shaped in part by an artist who left wartime Sarajevo. By 2012 he was living in the United Kingdom, a reminder that a person's story may not stop at one move.

Began his career as a concept artist at Nintendo.

2012: Concept work on The Avengers.

people.name: Amer Delić
body: In May 2003, in Athens, Georgia, a University of Illinois player beat Baylor's Benedikt Dorsch 6-4, 6-3 to win the NCAA singles championship. Amer Delić became the first Illinois player to win that title, and as of 2010 he was still the only one. The same season the Illini went undefeated and won the national team title.

In 1996, the year after the war ended, his family moved to Jacksonville, Florida. By ESPN's account, quoted in Tennis.com, he, his parents and his older sister arrived with $1,000 and four suitcases, and his sister translated for their parents.
At Illinois he was an All-American every season, and he and partner Graydon Oliver reached No. 1 in the national doubles rankings. He finished with a 92-33 singles record.

His career-high professional singles ranking was No. 60, in July 2007. At the 2009 Australian Open, ranked No. 220, he reached the third round and took Novak Djokovic to a final-set tiebreaker before losing. The Daily Illini called him Bosnian-born and American-raised.
keyFacts: 1996: Family moved from Bosnia to Jacksonville, Florida.
2003: NCAA singles champion and team champion with an undefeated Illinois.
July 2007: Career-high singles ranking of No. 60.
2009: Reached the third round of the Australian Open.

people.name: Sanela Diana Jenkins
body: Sanela Diana Jenkins was born in Sarajevo and was a university student when war reached the city. UCLA Law Magazine says she escaped at the height of the war. On her own website she writes that her brother was killed a few days before the Dayton Accords ended the fighting. "Nothing will bring him back," she writes.

In 2008 she and her husband, Roger Jenkins, gave UCLA School of Law $4 million to create the Sanela Diana Jenkins Clinic on International Justice. UCLA described it as the first endowed clinical program of its kind on the West Coast, with students working with prosecutors and judges on war crimes cases from Bosnia.

Her own site says the Sanela Diana Jenkins Human Rights Project followed at UCLA Law in 2009, directed by Professor Richard H. Steinberg, to support international criminal tribunals and train human rights lawyers. It also describes a foundation for Bosnia established in memory of Irnis Ćatić, and Haiti earthquake relief through J/P Haitian Relief Organization.

Her site described her in 2015 as founder and chief executive of the drinks company Neuro, living in Malibu, California. She is an example of a refugee who put personal loss to work in institutions built to last.
keyFacts: Born in Sarajevo; a university student when the war began.
2008: With Roger Jenkins, gave UCLA School of Law $4 million for a clinic on international justice.
2009: Sanela Diana Jenkins Human Rights Project established at UCLA Law, by her own site's account.
Founder of the company Neuro.
people.connectToWork: For someone who has lived through atrocity, how might public accountability matter alongside individual services, and how would you ask without pressing for their story?

people.name: Aida Šehović
body: On July 11, 2017, the anniversary of the Srebrenica genocide, thousands of small porcelain coffee cups covered Daley Plaza in downtown Chicago. Passersby helped set out the cups and fill them with Bosnian coffee. Each cup stood for one person killed at Srebrenica whose remains had been identified. The installation was ŠTO TE NEMA, a "nomadic monument" by the New York-based artist Aida Šehović.

She was born in Banja Luka in 1977 and was fifteen when war began in Bosnia. She earned a BA with honors from the University of Vermont and an MFA from CUNY Hunter College as a Jacob K. Javits Fellow. She first presented the work in a public square in Sarajevo in 2006, using cups collected with the Women of Srebrenica, a survivors' group.

For the next 15 years it appeared every July 11, in 15 cities including Boston and Chicago. Bosnian families donated the cups. By 2017 there were more than 7,500, and later more than 8,300. Volunteers encourage visitors to talk with one another, and there are no signs or flags. The traveling presentations ended in 2020, and she has been working with the Srebrenica-Potočari Memorial Center on a permanent version.

She was visiting artist in residence at Laumeier Sculpture Park in St. Louis in 2021. Her work has been shown at the Queens Museum, the Canadian Museum for Human Rights and the Atrocity Prevention Pavilion at the 58th Venice Biennale. It is a memorial built by many hands, one that brought Bosnian remembrance into American public squares.
keyFacts: 1977: Born in Banja Luka, Bosnia and Herzegovina (then Yugoslavia).
July 11, 2006: First presented ŠTO TE NEMA in Sarajevo.
2006 to 2020: Shown every July 11 in 15 cities; cups donated by Bosnian families.
2017: Presented at Daley Plaza in Chicago.
2021: Visiting artist in residence at Laumeier Sculpture Park, St. Louis.

people.name: Ermin Jusufović
body: AFP reported in 2024 that Ermin Jusufović was hit by a landmine in Bosnia a few days before his 16th birthday, more than a year after the war ended. He woke in a hospital bed and learned he had lost his leg.

He first played for Bosnia and Herzegovina in 2001, at the European Championships in Hungary, where the team won the title. World ParaVolley credits him with more than 15 years as a team captain and medals at five straight Paralympic Games, including bronze at Tokyo 2020. The team won gold at London 2012, and the International Paralympic Committee lists him in the gold medal match at Paris 2024, his sixth Games.
AFP reports he was voted most valuable player of the 2022 World Cup tournament. The same year World ParaVolley named him most valuable player at his club's Euroleague win.
He is on this page because of what he has done with his sport and for it, not because of what happened to him. He has no U.S. or Minnesota connection that could be found.
keyFacts: 1997: Landmine injury, by AFP's account, more than a year after the war ended.
2001: First played for Bosnia and Herzegovina.
2012: On the team that won Paralympic gold in London.
2022: Most valuable player at the World Cup, by AFP's account.
2024: Played in the gold medal match at the Paris Paralympics.
people.connectToWork: If an injury or impairment has a public side, such as a sport, a team or a cause, how would you ask whether that matters to this person, without assuming it does?

institutions.name: Intercultural Mutual Assistance Association
body: The Intercultural Mutual Assistance Association was founded in Rochester in 1984. The organization credits Robert "Bob" Jones III (1942–2011) as its founder. Ron Buzard, who began working in Rochester in the mid-1980s, led it for nearly 30 years before retiring in 2018.

In the 1990s refugees of the Bosnian War began arriving in Rochester. Armin Budimlic, who arrived from Bosnia in 1994, joined in 1998 to help fellow Bosnians resettle. As of October 2026 he is its executive director.

Today its mission is "building bridges between cultures through service, education, and access." Its programs are family services, health access and education, language services, a volunteer match program, victim services and whole family systems. It serves refugees and immigrants across southeast Minnesota.
keyFacts: 1984: Founded in Rochester.
1998: Armin Budimlic joined; he is now executive director.
Programs include language services, health access and victim services.
institutions.connectToWork: When a community-run organization does work your agency relies on, such as interpreting or health navigation, what does your agency do to pay for and credit that work?

institutions.name: Bosnian & Herzegovinian American Community Center
body: When the Bosnian War brought refugees to the United States, many came to Chicago. Community estimates from 2002, reported by the center, put the number who had settled there at about 40,000, mainly on the city's North Side.

In 1994 the Illinois Department of Human Services, with public and private agencies, founded the Bosnian Refugee Center. In 1997 it became an independent nonprofit, the Bosnian & Herzegovinian American Community Center. Its staff are Bosnian refugees of many backgrounds.

Its site lists homemaker and in-home care for qualified people with disabilities who live in Chicago, English lessons and civics classes, citizenship help, help with public benefits applications, and community events. Its permanent address is on West Argyle Street, and it has reported a temporary move along the same street because of construction.
keyFacts: 1994: Founded by the Illinois Department of Human Services as the Bosnian Refugee Center.
1997: Became an independent nonprofit.
Current programs include in-home care for qualified people with disabilities in Chicago.
institutions.connectToWork: When your agency starts a program for a new group, what would it take to hand it to the people it serves, including the money and decisions?

institutions.name: Center for Bosnian Studies
aliases: Center for Bosnian Studies, Saint Louis University
institutions.type: Scholarly center and oral history archive
body: St. Louis has about 60,000 Bosnians by the university's estimate, which it calls the largest such community outside Bosnia and Herzegovina. In 2006 Fontbonne University professor Benjamin Moore founded the Bosnia Memory Project to record the stories of survivors of the war and genocide, and of their families.

The project grew into a collection of oral histories, rare materials and digital archives. In 2020 it was renamed the Center for Bosnian Studies. In 2022, marking 30 years of Bosnia's independence from Yugoslavia, Fontbonne dedicated a new campus space to it. The university's release called it the only initiative of its kind in North America.

When Fontbonne announced it would close, Saint Louis University agreed to become the center's permanent home, starting in summer 2025. The March 2025 announcement said director Adna Karamehic-Oates and archivist Rebecca van Kniest would move with it. The center also presents an annual Civic Courage Award.
keyFacts: 2006: Founded at Fontbonne University as the Bosnia Memory Project.
2020: Renamed the Center for Bosnian Studies.
2025: Announced move to Saint Louis University.
institutions.connectToWork: Before you prepare material about a community's history, whose own recorded testimony could you read first, and how would you credit it?

institutions.name: Center for Victims of Torture
body: The Center for Victims of Torture grew out of a committee that Minnesota Governor Rudy Perpich assembled to recommend human rights initiatives. The committee proposed the first U.S. center for rehabilitative care for torture survivors, and it opened in St. Paul in 1985 with one counselor.

A University of Minnesota Human Rights Library page describes its individual and small-group counseling, psychosocial activities and training for religious leaders, teachers and caregivers. Its own site lists mental health counseling, group counseling, physiotherapy and social work among its services.

It is not a Bosnian organization. It appears here because the research on this page connects war trauma and disability, and because the clinical director of a St. Louis center for torture and war trauma survivors, a separate organization, spoke about Bosnian survivors' needs in a 2009 report.
keyFacts: 1985: Opened in St. Paul with one counselor.
Headquartered in St. Paul.
Serves survivors of torture from many countries.
institutions.connectToWork: When you are considering a referral for trauma care, how would you explain it so the person decides whether, when and how to use it?

disability.intro: This is background for preparing questions. It does not describe any person or family. Here, Bosnian means people from Bosnia and Herzegovina or with family ties there, who may identify as Bosniak, Croat, Serb, Jewish, mixed or none of these, and who may or may not be religious. No Minnesota-based study of how Bosnian Minnesotans understand disability was found. Most U.S. research is about war trauma, and most of it comes from St. Louis. The findings below come from small or specific samples, some decades old.
questions: How do you and your family describe what's going on? What words do you use for it at home?
Has anyone given you a diagnosis or a label? Who gave it to you, and has it helped or got in the way?
What would you want a label or assessment to open up for you? Is there anything you want it to avoid?
Some people's health changed because of the war. Would you like to tell me anything about that, or would you rather not talk about it today?
Who in your family helps with care, and who should be part of decisions? Is there anyone you do not want involved?
Have you had experiences with agencies, here or before you came here, that make it hard to trust services? What would you want to know about who I work for and who sees this information?
Would you prefer help on your own, in a group, or connected to a community or faith organization?
Are there supports you already use, including religious or traditional ones, that you would like us to know about?
Would you like an interpreter? Does the interpreter's background matter to you, and is there anyone you would not want interpreting?
Is there a word for your condition that you find hurtful, or one you prefer we use?

context.heading: War, injury and functioning in one 1996 survey
body: A Harvard Program in Refugee Trauma study published in JAMA in 1999 surveyed 534 randomly selected Bosnian adults in a refugee camp in Varaždin, Croatia, in 1996. It found 25.5 percent functionally disabled. People with symptoms of both depression and PTSD were more likely to report disability, as were adults 65 and older and people who had been through three to five traumatic events. It describes one camp, 30 years ago, and says nothing about anyone in Minnesota today.
So a person's disability may or may not be connected to the war. Let them decide whether to raise that, and how much to say.

sources.label: ScienceDaily summary of the Harvard Program in Refugee Trauma study, JAMA (1999)

context.heading: What studies have reported about mental health and stigma
body: In a 2009 St. Louis Public Radio report, researcher Ajlina Karamehic-Muratovic said that for Bosnians, having depression could equate to being "crazy", and described talking about mental health as off-limits and alcohol as one way people numbed pain. That is one researcher's account of one city at one time.

A 2016 survey of 117 Bosnian immigrants and refugees in the United States (Kulenovic, Loyola University Maryland) found they knew significantly more about mental illness and showed less stigmatizing behavior than Bosnians living in Bosnia. Acculturation did not explain the difference. Small percentages in both groups had sought treatment.

In a 2022 study, 62 second-generation Bosnian youth in St. Louis were interviewed. Authors reported that from the children's perspective their parents still faced mental health difficulties, that understanding of mental health was tied to stigma, and that intergenerational trauma might affect relationships. Plain, functional descriptions such as "trouble sleeping" or "needs help with stairs" may be easier to start with until a person uses other words.

sources.label: St. Louis Public Radio, Local Bosnians still struggle with post-traumatic stress (2009)
Kulenovic, Impact of acculturation on mental health stigma in Bosnian immigrants and refugees, Loyola University Maryland (2016)
Karamehic-Muratovic, Sichling and Doherty, Community Mental Health Journal (2022), abstract

context.heading: Family, generations and strengths
body: A 2007 conference abstract by Craig and Sossou surveyed 126 Bosnian refugees in a Midwestern state, a convenience sample, and interviewed seven who reported high well-being. In those interviews, the largest factor linked to resilience was hope drawn from the extended family. That is a strength to ask about, and it does not tell you who helps a particular person.

The 2009 St. Louis report described people who arrived in their 60s and 70s, spoke only Bosnian and were isolated, and children as young as five interpreting for parents. Nothing specific to disability was found on who decides in a family, so ask.

sources.label: Craig and Sossou, Society for Social Work and Research (2007), abstract
St. Louis Public Radio, Local Bosnians still struggle with post-traumatic stress (2009)

context.heading: Trust in services
body: The St. Louis report described a sense of betrayal by former neighbors and by institutions, including the United Nations, and a question put to providers: is somebody benefiting from our pain? A 2024 study of five Bosnian refugees in Melbourne, Australia, who had used mental health services (Karakas and du Plooy) found distrust of government-run services, concerns about how medication was prescribed, differing preferences for individual or group therapy, and a risk of re-traumatization. Five people cannot be generalized, and Melbourne is not Minnesota. Explain plainly who you work for, what is confidential and who benefits.
Use a trained interpreter, never a child. Because the community may be small and the war's divisions may matter to the person, ask about their preferences and confirm privacy.

sources.label: St. Louis Public Radio, Local Bosnians still struggle with post-traumatic stress (2009)
Karakas and du Plooy, International Journal of Migration, Health and Social Care (2024)

context.heading: What could not be found
body: This review found no Minnesota study, no Bosnian-language disability terms, no documented gender or decision-making norms in families affected by disability, no documented traditional healing practices, and no source documenting fate-based, moral or family-honor explanations of disability among Bosnians. It also found no culturally specific Bosnian disability organization in Minnesota. Do not assume any of these either way. The only Minnesota-specific source found is a 1999 MPR story saying that Bosnian war refugees had resettled across Minnesota and the Dakotas, some in cities and many in rural areas, including Pelican Rapids.

sources.label: MPR News, Bosnian refugees recall horror of war (April 19, 1999)

communityRoutes.name: Intercultural Mutual Assistance Association
communityRoutes.purpose: Rochester nonprofit with language services, health access and education, and victim services for refugees and immigrants in southeast Minnesota. Ask whether Bosnian interpreting is available when you call. 507-289-5960.

communityRoutes.name: Center for Victims of Torture
communityRoutes.purpose: St. Paul center for torture survivors of any background, with mental health counseling, group counseling, physiotherapy and social work among its listed services. Its site has a page for people looking for care. Ask what is available in Minnesota now.

organizations.intro: The sources found describe a small Bosnian presence in Minnesota, centered in the Twin Cities and Rochester. The Post Bulletin estimated 600 to 1,000 Bosnians in Rochester in 2024, and the Star Tribune counted about 1,200 members in one Minneapolis congregation in 2017. Neither is a census. No Bosnian-language media based in Minnesota was found, and no formal Bosnian association or mosque in Rochester. The list below is a starting point for learning, is not complete, and says nothing about who a person trusts.

entries.name: Islamic Community of Bosniaks (Minneapolis)
aliases: Islamic Center of Bosniaks in Minnesota
entries.purpose: The Star Tribune reported in 2017 that this congregation of about 1,200 had a mosque on Broadway Avenue, that Chisago County denied its cemetery permit 3-2, and that it had used Muslim sections of cemeteries in Roseville and Burnsville. The national directory lists an Islamic Center of Bosniaks in Minnesota, in Minneapolis, with no address. It is probably the same congregation, though neither source says so. The national body is a route to a current contact.
entries.linkLabel: Directory of local congregations, Islamic Community of Bosniaks in North America

entries.name: Catholic Charities (Rochester)
entries.purpose: Sponsored Elvis Budimlic and counted 67 Bosnian refugees relocated to Rochester from June 1993 through 1996, according to the Post Bulletin. It is not a Bosnian organization, and no current Bosnian-specific programs were found.
entries.linkLabel: Post Bulletin report on its 1990s resettlement work

entries.name: Rochester Srebrenica remembrance gatherings
entries.purpose: In July 2025, for the 30th anniversary of the genocide, people in Rochester held a first peace march around Cascade Lake and a daylong soccer tournament at Watson Sports Complex, KAAL reported. No formal organization was named. July may be a hard time for some people and a time of gathering for others, so ask.

entries.name: Stir Fry Express
entries.location: Duluth and Sioux Falls; Rochester location closed
entries.purpose: A self-serve restaurant run by a family from Bosnia, KTTC reported in February 2026. KTTC reported in October 2026 that the northwest Rochester location had permanently closed and that the owners' other locations were operating. A business, listed here as one sign of Bosnian entrepreneurship in the region.

entries.name: Islamic Community of Bosniaks in North America
entries.purpose: Founded in 2003. Umbrella body for about 60 local Bosniak congregations in four regions, with a Mufti as president. Its directory lists one Minnesota congregation.

entries.name: Congress of Bosniaks of North America
entries.purpose: Calls itself an independent, non-partisan national organization that represents Bosniak interests and promotes Bosniak cultural, historical, ethnic and religious heritage. It publishes news and commentary.

entries.name: Bosnian American Genocide Institute and Education Center
entries.purpose: A nonprofit that researches the 1992–1995 genocide in Bosnia and Herzegovina and teaches about genocide, the Holocaust and other crimes against humanity, with reconciliation as its stated aim.

entries.name: Advisory Council for Bosnia and Herzegovina
entries.purpose: Says it advances the interests of Bosnian Americans and U.S.–Bosnia relations, and works on civic engagement. GuideStar lists Ajla Delkić as executive director and president. The website it lists no longer leads to the organization, so start with GuideStar.

entries.name: Islamic and Cultural Center Bosniak
entries.purpose: Founded in 2005 by Bosnian refugees, described as the first Bosnian mosque in the Des Moines area, and the nearest large Bosniak center found outside Minnesota. Much conversation and Sunday school is in Bosnian, by Drake University's account.

entries.location: International, funded through the U.S. Agency for Global Media

entries.purpose: A national Bosnian-language weekly published from December 1997 to October 2014, in Astoria, New York, then St. Louis from 2006. It no longer publishes; its archive is a source for learning about the period.
